business.title: Morey Movement strengthens Sixmilebridge community through fitness
business.excerpt: A SIXMILEBRIDGE gym founded by first cousins Seadna and Chloe Morey is continuing to grow as the village’s population expands, with the owners keen to provide an accessible space for people of all fitness levels.
business.author: Michael Fitzgerald
business.caption: Seadna and Chloe Morey. Photograph: Joe Buckley
body: A SIXMILEBRIDGE gym founded by first cousins Seadna and Chloe Morey is continuing to grow as the village’s population expands, with the owners keen to provide an accessible space for people of all fitness levels.

Established in 2021 by former decorated inter-county stars Chloe and Seadna Morey, Morey Movement identified a gap in the local community for a facility focused on conditioning and general fitness and has gone from strength to strength since then.

“We have a massive interest in strength and conditioning,” Seadna explains. “We just wanted to bring something to the community in regards to keeping health and fitness as a priority for people and giving them an outlet to be able to come and exercise”.

The cousins currently run a sports camp for children in Sixmilebridge and said the idea for the gym developed naturally from their involvement in the local community. They subsequently completed their qualifications with Setanta College while continuing to work in their previous jobs before opening the facility.

Morey Movement operates on a pod based system, where members have access to their own squat rack and bench and are free to work out at their own pace rather than sharing with others. The gym is used by the Clare senior hurlers and has a contract with Sixmilebridge GAA to provide strength and conditioning for underage members, as well as providing a space for locals just looking to keep fit, showcasing the wide range of services and coaching available.

Chloe says that providing amenities for new and existing residents was an important consideration following The Bridge’s recent growth. “When a village grows like that numbers-wise, it's important that there's amenities for them as well. We didn't just want a run-of-the-mill gym. We wanted to create a space where everybody's welcome”, she explains.

This unique approach allows exercises to be tailored to each person's ability and experience, Seadna outlines. “You could have never come into a gym before in your life and when you come in the coach on the day would ensure that every single exercise is detailed towards your technique, your ability and we slowly build you up from there”, the two time All-Ireland and five-time Clare SHC winner highlights.

The owners have also noticed a growing focus among members on strength and overall wellbeing rather than simply losing weight in recent years as Chloe points out that “People these days now are more conscious of actually gaining strength. It's not all about losing weight. More often now people are realising how brilliant strength work is for their head more than anything and the improvement in their mental wellbeing”.

For Seadna, some of the most rewarding aspects of running the gym come from seeing small changes in people's everyday lives. “You might have someone come over to you and say ‘I did this for the first time in my life’ or ‘I don't feel my back pain anymore. It's the small things. It's not the athlete who's been out running, winning a race or anything like that. It's the small little changes in people's lives that you hear the stories about that kind of make it rewarding”, the Sixmilebridge native notes.

Looking ahead, the cousins hope to strengthen their links with other businesses and organisations in the village through events and initiatives. For now however, Seadna believes there are still plenty of people in the expanding village who are unaware of the gym and is determined to continue their progress. “The village is so big, I don't think a lot of people still know we're actually really here. It might not be for everyone, but getting in the door is the hardest part for people”, he explains.

business.title: Fast-tracking transport investment in Mid-West the big call from pre-Budget submission
business.excerpt: Three Chambers. One Connected Region. Karen Ronan Galway Chamber (CEO) , Shannon Chamber President, Helen Downes, and Sean Golden Limerick Chamber pictured as Galway Chamber, Shannon Chamber and Limerick Chamber are working together to strengthen a shared regional economy.
business.author: Páraic McMahon
body: Three Chambers. One Connected Region. Karen Ronan Galway Chamber (CEO) , Shannon Chamber President, Helen Downes, and Sean Golden Limerick Chamber pictured as Galway Chamber, Shannon Chamber and Limerick Chamber are working together to strengthen a shared regional economy.
TRANSPORT investment in the Mid-West needs to be fast-tracked to support economic growth, improve connectivity and promote balanced regional development.
Shannon Chamber, Galway Chamber and Limerick Chamber have compiled a joint pre-Budget 2027 proposal which has been submitted to the Department of Finance and the Department of Public Expenditure.

Urgent investment in roads, public transport, rail and aviation is needed to create a better-connected western region, the submission has highlighted. They said the projects are essential to supporting housing delivery, labour mobility, business investment and international competitiveness.

All three business groups are calling for increased investment in regional airports, highlighting the importance of international connectivity to economic growth, indigenous enterprise, foreign direct investment and tourism. They said investment in airports must be matched by improvements to the wider transport network to provide efficient access for businesses, workers and visitors.

The Chambers Ireland members are also calling for the accelerated delivery of strategic road projects, including the N19 Shannon Airport Access Road. They are seeking increased investment in public transport, including faster delivery of BusConnects in Galway and Limerick, as well as more integrated services linking cities, towns and communities across the region.

Continued investment in rail has been flagged by the Chambers as essential to a balanced transport strategy. They are calling for progress on a feasibility study for the proposed Shannon Rail Link, along with continued investment in the Western Rail Corridor to improve connectivity and support future sustainable transport needs. The business groups said the economic success of the western region depends on better connectivity between Galway, Shannon and Limerick.

They said an integrated transport network combining roads, public transport, aviation and rail would help unlock the region's economic potential and strengthen its competitiveness nationally and internationally.

Shannon Chamber Chief Executive Helen Downes said, “Shannon Airport, our cities and our growing towns are key economic assets. Ensuring they are connected through a modern and efficient transport network is fundamental to unlocking future growth opportunities. Investment in projects such as the N19 Shannon Airport Access Road and enhanced public transport services will deliver significant benefits for businesses, employees and communities across the region”.

Galway Chamber Chief Executive Karen Ronan said successive governments had committed to balanced regional development, but investment had not kept pace. “The west has the enterprise base, the talent and the ambition to drive national economic growth, but it needs the infrastructure to match. A connected region is essential if we are to deliver housing, improve labour mobility, attract investment and enhance quality of life. Budget 2027 must prioritise delivery of the strategic transport projects that have been talked about for too long”.

Limerick Chamber Chief Economist and Director of Policy Seán Golden said investment in transport connectivity must be viewed as a national competitiveness priority. “The continued growth of the western region depends on our ability to move people efficiently between where they live, work, study and do business. Strategic investment in roads, public transport and rail infrastructure, combined with strong international connectivity through Shannon Airport, will strengthen links across the region, support enterprise growth and enhance Ireland's attractiveness as a location for investment”.
Beyond transport infrastructure, the three Chambers' Pre-Budget 2027 submissions contain a wide range of proposals aimed at strengthening regional competitiveness and supporting economic growth.

Shannon Chamber is seeking increased investment the OneShannonHub regeneration project, alongside accelerated investment in offshore renewable energy infrastructure, housing delivery, workforce skills and artificial intelligence.

Galway Chamber is seeking increased investment in housing-enabling infrastructure, greater funding certainty for major capital projects and increased investment in skills, innovation and artificial intelligence and local authority funding reform.

Limerick Chamber is calling for measures to boost enterprise competitiveness, speed up housing delivery, regenerate Limerick city centre and develop the Shannon Estuary as a strategic hub for energy and industry.

business.title: Shannon was fastest growing airport in Ireland for June
business.excerpt: SHANNON AIRPORT was the fastest growing airport in Ireland for the month of June.
business.author: Páraic McMahon
body: SHANNON AIRPORT was the fastest growing airport in Ireland for the month of June.

New figures published by the Irish Tourism Industry Confederation (ITIC) show Shannon Airport recorded the strongest year-on-year passenger growth among Ireland's major airports in June, with traffic increasing by 14 percent compared to the same month last year.
According to the ITIC research, traffic increased at Shannon by 14 percent which surpassed Dublin Airport’s two percent growth while Cork Airport recorded a reduction in activity of three percent.

Visitors from the European Union are up eight percent nationally, an increase in arrivals from the United Kingdom of five percent was recorded while there are less people arriving in Ireland from the United States of America and Canada, the figures dropping seven percent in twelve months.
Occupancy levels for hotels are down 1.2 percent in June 2026 compared with June 2025 while Air BnB occupancy dipped by three percent.

CEO of the Shannon Airport Group, Ray O’Driscoll said, “We are encouraged to see the recently published industry figures from ITIC showing Shannon Airport recording the strongest year-on-year passenger growth among Ireland's major airports in June. This provides further evidence of the positive impact of our ongoing route development strategy and the strong partnerships we continue to build with our airline partners”.

New routes and additional aircraft are aiding the growth, he stated. “The introduction of a fourth based Ryanair aircraft this year, together with four new services to Madrid, Rome, Warsaw and Poznań, has played a significant role in driving this 14% growth. The new Discover Airlines route to Frankfurt, together with increased frequencies on the Aer Lingus Boston service also made an important contribution, while providing passengers with even greater choice and connectivity through Shannon Airport.

“We are very proud of Shannon Airport's growing network, which now offers the largest number of routes in 17 years, and of the role we play in supporting tourism and economic growth across the region, the West of Ireland and along the Wild Atlantic Way”.

business.title: Over 65k passengers forecast for August Bank Holiday at Shannon Airport
business.excerpt: MORE THAN 65,000 passengers are expected through Shannon Airport over the August Bank Holiday weekend in what is a seven percent increase for the same period in 2025.
business.author: Páraic McMahon
body: MORE THAN 65,000 passengers are expected through Shannon Airport over the August Bank Holiday weekend in what is a seven percent increase for the same period in 2025.

A strong Bank Holiday forecast is in line with Shannon Airport’s continued growth in 2026. The airport welcomed 1.17 million passengers during the first six months of the year, a 12% increase on the same period in 2025.

Growth has been supported by the airport's expanded schedule, which this year includes 40 routes, its largest route network in 17 years, together with increased European and transatlantic capacity. New services to destinations including Rome, Madrid, Warsaw, Poznan and Frankfurt, along with additional frequencies on key routes, have further strengthened connectivity for passengers across the region.

Ray O'Driscoll, CEO of The Shannon Airport Group, said: “We are looking forward to welcoming more than 65,000 passengers through Shannon Airport over the August Bank Holiday period, reflecting the strong demand we continue to see from both business and leisure travellers and the growing appeal of our expanded route network”.

He continued, “The strong growth we are seeing in passenger numbers is being matched by growing confidence in Shannon Airport as an aviation and economic hub. Ryanair's recent announcement of plans for a €50 million investment in a new maintenance facility and Engineering Academy at Shannon, supporting more than 400 highly skilled jobs, is a major endorsement of the airport, the region and the opportunities for future growth.
“We remain focused on enhancing the passenger experience, investing in our infrastructure and supporting tourism, connectivity and economic growth across the region,” O’Driscoll added.
Shannon Airport has continued to invest in infrastructure and customer experience improvements, including upgrades currently underway in the arrivals area and baggage hall.

Passengers travelling this August Bank Holiday are encouraged to plan ahead and arrive in good time for their flights. Shannon Airport offers five car parks located between a 30-second and seven-minute walk from the terminal building, while the Shannon Airport App and pre-booked parking options can help make journeys even more convenient.

business.title: Ryanair to create 400 jobs in Shannon as part of €50m investment
business.excerpt: RYANAIR has announced it is to make a €50m investment at Shannon Airport which will create 400 jobs.
business.author: Páraic McMahon
body: RYANAIR has announced it is to make a €50m investment at Shannon Airport which will create 400 jobs.
This investment will see the construction of a new four-bay aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) hangar and an Engineering Academy at Shannon Airport resulting in 400 jobs.

Planning has been sought by Ryanair on a 6.7-acre site on the airfield at Shannon Airport. Subject to planning approval, the facility will become the airline's largest aircraft maintenance operation in Ireland and further strengthen Shannon's position as one of Europe's leading aviation centres.
Senior management of Ryanair were in Shannon on Thursday to make the announcement along with Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, Peter Burke (FG).

Already Ryanair operates a three-bay aircraft maintenance facility employing more than 200 people in Shannon Airport. Ryanair has operated from Shannon Airport since 1987 and remains one of the airport's most important airline partners, contributing significantly to connectivity, tourism and employment across the west of Ireland. This summer, Ryanair operates a record 30 routes from Shannon and has increased seat capacity by 15% compared with the same period last year.

Construction is expected to commence in early 2027 with the facility expected to enter operation in late 2028, subject to planning approval. The proposed new facility will comprise more than 15,000m² of aircraft maintenance and ancillary space.

Enterprise Ireland are supporting the development of the Engineering Academy. which will see the creation of 80 new apprenticeship roles will be created and support the training of over 400 additional aircraft mechanics between 2027 and 2031.

CEO of Ryanair, Eddie Wilson stated, “This project is about jobs, skills and growth. Shannon already plays an important role in maintaining Ryanair's fleet, and this expansion will create hundreds of highly skilled engineering jobs while training the next generation of aircraft mechanics in Ireland. This major new facility will not only increase Ryanair’s aircraft maintenance capacity at Shannon but will also include a new Engineering Academy, providing dedicated training facilities for up to 80 apprentices, training over 400 mechanics between 2027 and 2031”.

Minister Burke welcomed the announcement which he said was “creating high quality jobs here in Shannon, is very welcome and demonstrates the continued success of this Irish company’s performance internationally. The government through Enterprise Ireland is committed to scaling and building Irish multinationals that will help drive the Irish economy and our competitive advantage forward. Ryanair’s announcement today is evidence of that Irish multinational ambition in action, and we are delighted to support them on their Shannon expansion plans to include the establishment of a dedicated Ryanair Engineering Academy”.

Enterprise Ireland CEO, Jenny Melia stated, “The company’s investment in skills and training in Shannon is particularly significant, supporting the development of specialist talent and helping to address critical skills needs across the aviation sector. This investment further strengthens Ireland’s position as a centre of excellence for aviation. Ambitious companies like Ryanair exemplify Enterprise Ireland’s vision that Irish globally focused companies will be the primary driver of our economy. Enterprise Ireland looks forward to continuing to work with the Ryanair team as they pursue their expansion plans, grow their international customer base, and create high-quality employment opportunities in Ireland.”

Minister for Transport, Darragh O’Brien (FF), stated, “Our ambition and vision for the State-owned Shannon Airport Group to strengthen its aerospace industry cluster at Shannon Airport is further enhanced by this investment, which will also bring a significant number of new jobs to the airport campus making an important contribution to the economy in the mid-west region. This investment also reflects Ireland’s position as a global leader in aviation and reinforces our reputation as a leading international hub for the aerospace industry.”

Ray O’Driscoll, CEO of The Shannon Airport Group commented, “Ryanair's proposal to invest at Shannon is a powerful endorsement of Shannon Airport, our aviation ecosystem and the wider region. From the birthplace of aircraft leasing, Shannon has grown into a global hub for aviation, spanning aircraft maintenance, engineering, leasing and aviation services. Today, Shannon Airport and the adjacent Shannon Airport Business Park together support Ireland's largest aviation cluster, with almost 100 companies operating across the campus. The airport’s 10 aircraft hangars which are used for aircraft MRO, aircraft painting and general aviation activities are further evidence of the breadth and strength of Shannon’s aviation sector.

“The scale of Ryanair's proposal reflects the depth of aviation expertise, engineering capability and talent that has developed here over decades. We are proud of our long-standing relationship with Ryanair and look forward to supporting its ambitions at Shannon. This significant investment by Ryanair, with support from Enterprise Ireland, will not only create highly skilled employment opportunities but will also help develop the next generation of aviation talent, further strengthening the region’s skills base and supporting continued economic growth,” O’Driscoll added.

In a statement to The Clare Echo, Clare TD Cathal Crowe (FF) described it as “game changing” for Shannon Airport. “This is a very significant investment in Shannon Airport and a realisation of the potential of the airport to play an even more significant role in international aviation. The announcement of a significant number of new jobs will be very welcome to the airport itself but also to the surrounding communities which will benefit from the influx of these new highly skilled employees.

He added, “Whilst this announcement is not expected to directly create new routes in and out of Shannon, the scale of the investment which Ryanair will be announcing will be game changing for Shannon Airport and the operations there. This investment is an investment in the very future of Shannon Airport”.

In November, Ryanair announced the addition of four new routes from Shannon to Madrid, Poznań, Rome and Warsaw along with reiterating their previously announced plans to have a fourth based aircraft in Shannon. Chief Operating Officer of Ryanair, Jason McGuinness said it represented a €345m investment.

business.title: Top marks for Newmarket-on-Fergus' Callum Mc in accountancy exams
business.excerpt: NEWMARKET-ON-FERGUS’ Callum McNamara has ranked among the best in Ireland and the world with his accountancy exams.
business.author: Páraic McMahon
body: NEWMARKET-ON-FERGUS’ Callum McNamara has ranked among the best in Ireland and the world with his accountancy exams.

An Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA) student at Dublin-based online college, Accountancy School, Callum finished first in Ireland and third in the world in his Strategic Business Reporting exam. In addition, he also ranked first in Ireland and sixth globally in Advanced Financial Management.
This is the second consecutive set of professional exams where Callum has placed first in Ireland for a subject. He works as an accountant with Xeinadin at their Galway offices.

Viewing his results in context, of the worldwide number of 500,000 ACCA students, approximately 8,000 of whom study in Ireland, Callum was among 28 fellow Accountancy School students to finish first in Ireland. All were recognised for their achievements at a ceremony in Dublin recently.

Accountancy School managing director, Dave O’Donoghue said, “ACCA is a globally recognised accountancy qualification, and the key to a hugely rewarding career in accountancy and financial management, here in Ireland and internationally. At a time when employers worldwide are actively seeking qualified accounting talent, ACCA trainees, affiliates and members continue to benefit from strong demand for their skills and excellent career prospects”.

Twenty five year old Callum is a former footballer with Treaty Utd and Galway Utd. He made 56 appearances for Treaty in their first two seasons in the League of Ireland before moving to Galway but injury deprived him the chance of featuring for the Tribesmen during his year-long stint with them.

Prior to this, Callum caught the eye with his home club, Newmarket Celtic. He began training with the club’s A team at the age of fifteen and represented the Newmarket Celtic A side for two seasons before signing for Treaty. He is a past pupil of Scoil na Maighdine Mhuire and St Caimin’s Community School while he also graduated from TUS.

business.title: Gas Networks Ireland appoint Kildysart's Ginnane as CLO for gas reserve project
business.excerpt: GAS NETWORKS Ireland have appointed Kildysart native John Ginnane as Community Liaison Officer for the controversial Strategic Gas Emergency Reserve (SGER) project.
business.author: Páraic McMahon
body: GAS NETWORKS Ireland have appointed Kildysart native John Ginnane as Community Liaison Officer for the controversial Strategic Gas Emergency Reserve (SGER) project.

Selected as the site in November for Ireland’s new strategic gas emergency reservice (SGER), the Cahercon facility is to create 300 jobs, a sixth of which will become full-time posts. The gas reserve will be delivered in the form of a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU), which will be owned and operated on behalf of the State by Gas Networks Ireland.

Environmental groups have raised concerns with the development of the gas reserve while the move to appoint Kildysart’s John will help to diffuse any potential tensions with local organisations and residents.

Well-known in the locality, John has been actively involved in a wide range of community initiatives and committees over many years, including the Playground Committee, local GAA Club, Parish Council, the Board of Management at the National School and is the current Chairperson of the Kildysart Community Centre.

Professionally, John has over 35 years’ experience working with ESB at Moneypoint Generating Station, where he developed a strong reputation for reliability, clear communication, and working effectively with stakeholders. This experience, combined with his community insight, uniquely positions him for the role, according to Gas Networks Ireland.

As Community Liaison Officer, John will act as the main point of contact between Gas Networks Ireland and the local community. He will be regularly present in the area, meeting residents, attending local events and meetings, and ensuring that information about the SGER project is shared openly and transparently, while also bringing community feedback directly to the project team.

Of his new role, John said, “I’m pleased to take on this role and to work closely with the local community. Open communication and trust are very important to me, and I look forward to engaging with people, listening to their views, and ensuring their voices are heard throughout the project”. Gas Networks Ireland said the appointment reflects its commitment to meaningful engagement, transparency, and ongoing dialogue with the communities living closest to the proposed development.

Community members who wish to speak with John or have queries about the SGER project can contact him directly at: johnginnane@gasnetworks.ie and can find out more about the project by visiting Strategic Gas Emergency Reserve | Gas Networks Ireland.

business.title: Minister approves pay increase for O'Driscoll & Considine
business.excerpt: SHANNON AIRPORT Group’s CEO has received a €35,000 increase in pay to €225,000.
business.author: The Clare Echo
body: SHANNON AIRPORT Group’s CEO has received a €35,000 increase in pay to €225,000.

That is according to figures released by the Department of Transport which has confirmed that the Minister for Transport, Darragh O’Brien (FF) has now sanctioned pay increased for eight CEOs of commercial state bodies.
The cumulative pay increase for the eight CEOs totals €333,000.

Minister O’Brien sanctioned the pay increase for the role of Shannon Airport Group CEO in January of this year but the Department at the time did not make public the pay increase as the Shannon Group was in the process of appointing a new CEO at the time.
In April, the board of the Shannon Airport Group announced that then interim CEO, Ray O'Driscoll has been appointed full-time to the job.
Mr O’Driscoll had been serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer of The Shannon Airport Group since September 2025, following the departure of former CEO Mary Considine.
The €225,000 salary does not include pension contributions and other taxable benefits.
The 2025 remuneration package for the role of CEO at the Shannon Group totalled €264,983 made up of the then salary of €190,000, pension contributions and other taxable benefits of €74,983.
The pay rise for the CEO of the Shannon Group arises from a Government review of the pay for CEOs of commercial state bodies.
Mr O’Driscoll’s predecessor in the role at Shannon Group, Mary Considine has also benefited from the pay overhaul for CEOs at commercial state bodies.
Ms Considine is now CEO at Iarnród Éireann and the pay for the role of CEO at Iarnród Éireann increased from €225,000 to €300,000 in August of last year.

In total, Minister O’Brien has sanctioned pay rises for CEO for eight commercial state bodies and along with the Shannon Group, they are Iarnród Éireann, Bus Éireann, Bus Átha Cliath, CIÉ, the Dublin Port Company, the Port of Waterford Company and the Port of Cork company.
The pay awards come against the background of there being no systematic review of CEO remuneration since 2011 and any increase in salary since that time has taken place on a case-by-case basis.

Following a Senior Posts Remuneration Committee (SPRC) performing a review of the remuneration arrangements for the CEOs of commercial state bodies, board of the commercial state bodies can send proposals to the relevant line Department setting out the proposed new salary and supporting rationale.

The relevant line Department then undertakes an assessment of the proposal, and the relevant Minister subsequently considers the Board’s recommendation, the Department’s analysis, and input from NewERA before making a final decision.
Following this process, recommendations by the relevant Minister are then submitted to Minister for Public Expenditure, Jack Chambers

Prior to stepping into the interim role at the Shannon Group, Mr O’Driscoll served as Deputy CEO and Chief Operating Officer, bringing extensive leadership experience across airport operations, commercial development, strategic planning and organisational governance.
Mr O'Driscoll first joined The Shannon Airport Group in 2014 as Managing Director of Shannon Commercial Enterprises, the Group’s commercial property division.

business.title: Element Six to seek refunds on Trump tariffs as revenues dip to $147.5m
business.excerpt: SHANNON based industrial diamond manufacturer, Element Six is going to work with its tax partners to seek refunds on US tariffs as soon as possible.
business.author: The Clare Echo
body: SHANNON based industrial diamond manufacturer, Element Six is going to work with its tax partners to seek refunds on US tariffs as soon as possible.
That is according to new accounts for Element Six Ltd which show that the imposition of the Trump tariffs last year contributed to revenues declining by 13 percent from $169.95m to $147.5m (€129.1m).
The firm recorded an operating loss of $4.92m (€4.3m) and this followed the company enjoying an operating profit of $560,000 in 2024, a negative swing of $5.48m.

The firm last September paid out dividends of $10m and this followed a $10m dividend payout in 2024. The directors state that both the company and the group were impacted by US tariffs and geo-political uncertainty in 2025.

Providing additional commentary on the performance of the Shannon unit, the directors state that uncertainties in global markets, the imposition of tariffs in certain markets, and broader macroeconomic headwinds resulted in a 13.2 percent decline in turnover compared with the prior year.
The directors’ report adds that “in response to these conditions, the directors continued to maintain a strong focus on cost control and operational efficiency across the business”.

In a post balance sheet, the directors state that on February 20th of this year, the US Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Power Act (IEEPA) does not authorise the President of the US to impose tariffs.

They state, “However, no mechanism to claim refunds was decided. No adjustment has been made in the financial statements for this although the company will work with our tax partners to seek refunds as soon as possible”.
The markets mainly served with industrial diamond and related products are the United States of America, China, Japan and all countries within the EU.
Element Six Ltd reduced its operating losses of $4.9m to a pre-tax loss of $645,000 through chiefly a dividend received of $3.33m and net interest received of $949,000.
The firm recorded a post-tax loss of $830,000 after incurring a corporation tax charge of $185,000.

Numbers employed last year declined from 413 to 405, that included 190 agency workers. The 215 directly employed workers made up of 104 in production, 63 in finance and administration, 27 in engineering and 21 in sales and marketing.
Total staff costs, including the cost of agency workers, increased from $31.34m to $33.2m that included $29.09m in wages and salaries.

The profit takes account of non-cash depreciation and amortisation costs of $5.45m. The company’s R&D spend totalled $4.45m compared to $6.94m in 2024. The profit also took account of a $1.67m write down and a foreign exchange loss of $1.8m.
Aggregate pay to directors last year totalled $812,000, down from $910,000 paid out in 2024.

The directors state that the principal risks and uncertainties include low-cost competition from Eastern European and Asian suppliers, commodity price, global tariffs uncertainties, fluctuations impacting consumer demand and fluctuating currency exchange rates
At the end of December last year, the firm had shareholder funds of $110.09m that included accumulated profits of $106.09m.

business.title: Summer season to see Shannon welcome hundreds of thousands of passengers
business.excerpt: HUNDREDS of thousands of passengers will fly through Shannon Airport over the coming weeks with schools finished, exams completed and the summer holiday season in full swing.
business.author: Páraic McMahon
body: HUNDREDS of thousands of passengers will fly through Shannon Airport over the coming weeks with schools finished, exams completed and the summer holiday season in full swing.

Planning ahead is the secret to hassle-free travel, Airport Director at Shannon Airport, Niall Kearns stated. “We know travel can sometimes feel a little stressful at this time of year, but a bit of planning really helps people relax from the moment they arrive,” he said. “Once everything is organised, people can switch straight into holiday mode. That's what Shannon Airport is all about, making it easy so that our passengers don’t have to wait until they land for that holiday feeling to kick in.”

With five car parks, all within a short walk of the terminal, passengers are encouraged to pre-book online. Travellers can also use the Shannon Airport App to pin their car's location, avoiding that dreaded post-holiday search of the car park.

When it comes to holiday essentials, the smartphone sits high on the list. Before leaving home, make sure your boarding pass is downloaded and accessible offline, and keep important travel documents easily to hand.

“We're all dependent on our phones these days when it comes to holidays – boarding passes, hotel booking confirmations, transfer details – they're all there,” Niall said. “The best approach is to follow your airline's guidance and ensure your boarding pass is available offline through the airline app or your phone's wallet. Some travellers keep copies of their other important travel information in more than one place and share key details with those in their group, just in case a battery dies or a phone goes missing”.

While airport security is often the part of the journey travellers worry about most, Shannon Airport says there’s no need to stress. The advice is straightforward: empty pockets, remove jackets, hoodies, belts and over-the-ankle footwear before screening, and keep liquids, gels and aerosols to 100ml or under. At Shannon Airport all liquids and electronics can stay inside your cabin bag.

Screening Supervisor Katie Duggan-Hastings explained, “There's no need to be nervous about security screening. There is clear signage before you come through to the area and our team is always available to help. We want every passenger to have a relaxed, positive experience”.

“Making travel accessible and comfortable for everyone is a key focus at Shannon Airport,” Kearns added. “We have a range of dedicated services in place to support passengers who need anything from full assistance to just a little extra help. We'd encourage anyone who might benefit to make use of them.”

Shannon Airport offers PRM (Passengers with Reduced Mobility) support, a Sensory Room, a Changing Places facility and participates in the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower programme. It is also one of only two airports in Europe recognised as ‘Age Friendly’ by the World Health Organisation, helping to ensure every passenger's journey is as comfortable and supported as possible.

While Shannon Airport is known for its ease of use, passengers are still advised to allow two hours before scheduled departure time for European flights and three hours before transatlantic trips. That allows time to browse its unique Duty Free with over 150 Irish and local brands, enjoy a coffee, cold drink or bite to eat and start the holiday at a more relaxed pace.

With 40 destinations on offer this year, full US Preclearance, short walking distances and friendly staff, Shannon Airport has been named Ireland's top airport brand for the past three years and achieves a 90% “recommend to a friend” rating. As it prepares to welcome passengers from across the country during the busy summer season, the message is simple: a little preparation before travelling can really help make the journey easier and more enjoyable. “Summer travel should be about looking forward to the destination, not worrying about airport logistics,” Niall stated. “A little preparation can go a long way and our team is always on hand to help make sure every holiday gets off to a great start”.

arts.title: Doolin's distinctive heritage & legacy of Stiofáin Uí Ealaoire to be celebrated
arts.excerpt: STORIES and the legacy of Doolin storyteller Stiofáin Uí Ealaoire will be celebrated in North Clare this week.
arts.author: Páraic McMahon
body: STORIES and the legacy of Doolin storyteller Stiofáin Uí Ealaoire will be celebrated in North Clare this week.
Stiofáin’s stories will be brought back to life at a free event for over sixteens in Doolin Community Centre n Thursday (August 20th) at 19:30.

Local storytellers will take centre stage to celebrate storytelling, heritage and community. The evening is the culmination of a series of storytelling workshops facilitated by renowned storyteller and performer Aindrias de Staic of the Burren Storytelling Centre, with the assistance of Alysh Doyle and members of the Doolin Heritage Project.

During the workshops, local participants have explored the stories, characters, traditions and storytelling heritage of Doolin, learning how to bring this material to life for a modern audience. The event is funded by The Heritage Council and is supported by The Doolin Heritage Project.

At the heart of the project is the work and legacy of Stiofáin whose stories and knowledge form an important part of Doolin’s cultural heritage. Rather than simply preserving these stories as part of the past, the project gives a new generation the opportunity to explore them, learn from them and share them in their own voices.

Aindrias has worked with locals to develop their storytelling skills, helping them to transform material from Doolin’s rich oral tradition into a live performance. The result will be an evening where Doolin’s stories are told by local people, for the local community, while celebrating the storytelling tradition that has helped to give Doolin its distinctive cultural identity.

“This is about keeping the stories alive,” Andrias told The Clare Echo. “Stiofáin Uí Ealaoire behind a wealth of stories and a wonderful storytelling tradition. Through this project, those stories are being passed on to a new generation, giving local people the skills and confidence to bring them onto the stage and share them again”.

Born in Ballycullaun in December 1858, Stiffen attended school irregularly for two to three years, his parents Mícheál Ó hEalaoire and Cáit Ní Dhanachair were both storytellers. Like his father, he became a farmer and was involved locally with the Land League. He died on May 4th 1944 and never married. He became well known as a storyteller from around 1930, when the renowned folklorist James Delargy got to know him. Stories collected from him by Delargy were published in Daithí Ó hÓgáin (ed.), Leabhar Stiofáin Uí Ealaoire (Dublin, 1981). In addition, a good deal of material collected from him is housed in the National Folklore Collection, UCD, along with an account by him of his life, and an obituary by Seán Mac Mathúna.

arts.title: Feakle Festival hits the high notes with 'biggest festival ever'
arts.excerpt: FEAKLE experienced its biggest ever traditional music festival with over 10,000 visitors coming through East Clare to sample the craic and ceol.
arts.author: Páraic McMahon
arts.caption: Photograph: Ruthie Griffin.
body: FEAKLE experienced its biggest ever traditional music festival with over 10,000 visitors coming through East Clare to sample the craic and ceol.
Held from Wednesday August 5th to Monday August 10th, the Feakle Festival hit the high notes with 250 campervans perched up in the East Clare village and its surrounds.
Organisers say the festival brought more than 10,000 people to East Clare and all events were sold out.

Over 400 people partook in the workshops as the Feakle Festival recorded its most successful week which also provided an economic boost to local businesses, particularly those in the hospitality and pub sector.

Speaking to The Clare Echo, Cllr Pat Hayes (FF) who has had a lifelong involvement with the festival, commented, “this was the biggest festival ever, we were blessed with the weather. With the scramble for tickets for different events, people said it was a bit like Electric Picnic or trying to get tickets for an All-Ireland final”.

Hailing the 2026 festival as “a phenomenal success,” Cllr Hayes stated, “the economic value of the festival to Feakle, East Clare and the entire county is huge. The amount of people who flew in from all over the world, they came from Japan, England, Brussels and China to be here, to immerse themselves in East Clare. The celebration of the Tulla Ceili Band set the tone for the week, event after event was sold out from then on. The volume of people who stayed in houses, campervans, tents, 300 people stayed in campervans and tents outside of them staying in Ennis and Gort, it makes a huge return and keeps businesses afloat for whole year”.
With 2027 marking the 40th Feakle Festival, Cllr Hayes said the success “lays down a marker to have more programming and keep the uniqueness of the Feakle Festival”.

He continued, “Feakle is a living village, it is not a tourist village, it recreates itself for the week, it will never be Doolin, Westport or those places, it is uniqueness that it can keep recreate as a living village for the week. The regular sessions that take place in Peppers every Wednesday and Shortts every Thursday is what its about. People want to come back to where the music is from, a lot of people went to Belfast for a day or two of the Fleadh and then did the week in Feakle or the oppoisite, people didn’t want to miss it. The welcome really comes across, you are getting real Ireland, it isn’t commercial”.

On the clash with Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann, Cllr Hayes said, “It doesn’t affect us at all, a couple of years ago we thought about changing it but a lot of musicians aren’t into competitions or don’t travel to larger towns for Fleadhs. If we could bottle what is in Feakle, that is what people come for, the unique experience of Feakle doesn’t come close to a Fleadh, I am not taking from the Fleadh, it had one million visitors but there’s something special in Feakle”.

Eightieth anniversary celebrations for the Tulla Céilí Band and the launch of an anniversary CD kicked off the festival while ninety years of the Tulla Pipe Band were also celebrated. Tulla fiddler, Sorcha Costelloe took a look at the past and future in a presentation titled ‘Looking back while moving forward: The past, present and future of the East Clare Music Tradition’.

Workshops were held on Thursday, Friday and Saturday morning where the tutors included the iconic Martin Hayes, Mary McNamara, Claire Keville, Jack Talty, Terence O’Reilly, Nuala Kennedy and Páraic Mac Donnchadha, Sold-out concerts were a constant of the festival.
Gallery of photographs by Ruthie Griffin.

arts.title: Méabh, Mark & Shane to fly the Clare flag at Rose of Tralee
arts.excerpt: SIXMILEBRIDGE’s Méabh Holland is bidding to become only the second Clare woman to win the Rose of Tralee while two Clare men will serve as escorts for the famed festival.
arts.author: Páraic McMahon
body: SIXMILEBRIDGE’s Méabh Holland is bidding to become only the second Clare woman to win the Rose of Tralee while two Clare men will serve as escorts for the famed festival.
Tralee welcomes the Roses and Escorts for the 67th festival with the Sixmilebridge woman an outside contender to be named the Rose of Tralee.
Twenty two year old Méabh was selected as the Clare Rose at the beginning of May, prevailing in a contest of fourteen to succeed Feakle’s Aisling O’Connor who made it to the Dome in August 2023.

A primary school teacher, Méabh has a love for her native language and spent her summers teaching Gaeilge in Connemara. She teaches the concertina with Music Generation Clare and The Irish Concertina Orchestra.

Ladbrokes have Méabh at 25/1 to win outright. Nicola McGeady of Ladbrokes commented, “Clare have only won the competition once, almost 60 years ago. However, Clare locals are backing their Rose to go all the way this year”.
Adding to the Clare contingent in Tralee are escorts, Shane Harrison from Quin and Barefield’s Mark Lynch.

Twenty four year old Shane is a graduate of the University of Limerick who now works as a site engineer in Galway. “Home has always been a huge part of who I am. Growing up in Clare has given me a great appreciation for community, and I've been fortunate to spend most of my life playing hurling with Clooney/Quin GAA Club. Whether I'm on the pitch, helping out on the farm, or catching up with family and friends, I'm happiest when I'm surrounded by good people,” he said.

“Away from work, I love music, travelling, and experiencing new places and cultures. One of my biggest goals is to visit as many countries as I can. I enjoy making the most of every opportunity, having a laugh, and never saying no to a new adventure. I'm really looking forward to the Rose of Tralee Festival as I think It's a fantastic opportunity to meet people from all over the world and make lifelong memories. Most of all, I'm excited to embrace the experience and have plenty of craic along the way,” Shane added.
A pharmacist at Marry Jo Duffy’s in Ennis, Mark quipped that he spends his working hours “reading impossible penmanship and gently explaining that antibiotics won't cure a hangover”.

There will be a strong Clare spirit in Tralee, the twenty nine year old outlined, “Outside the pharmacy, I'm a massive fan of Clare GAA and Munster Rugby, and can usually otherwise be found at a music festival or concert. Growing up with a younger sister and working almost exclusively with women, I consider myself a master in the art of patience, a trait that will come in remarkably handy in Tralee. I'm swapping the dispensary for the Dome to bring proper Banner spirit to Kerry and ensure my Rose has an absolute blast, while entertaining with my impressions and dry wit”.
The Rose of Tralee airs on RTÉ One and RTÉ Player on Monday 17 August and Tuesday 18 August from 8pm.

arts.title: Ambitious arts plan to repurpose vacant buildings in Galway
arts.excerpt: Galway County Council has adopted a new five-year Arts Plan that will see increased investment in artists through grants and bursaries, the repurposing of vacant buildings as arts spaces and investment in arts infrastructure to improve access to cultural activities across County Galway.
arts.author: Páraic McMahon
body: Galway County Council has adopted a new five-year Arts Plan that will see increased investment in artists through grants and bursaries, the repurposing of vacant buildings as arts spaces and investment in arts infrastructure to improve access to cultural activities across County Galway.
The five-year strategy also commits to strengthening support for arts venues and festivals, developing a countywide Cultural Arts Trail and establishing Tuam as a long-term creative hub.

Titled ‘A Place to Create, A Place to Live’, the plan sets out a roadmap for the development of the arts over the next five years, with a focus on supporting artists, expanding participation, improving cultural infrastructure and ensuring the arts are accessible to communities throughout the county.
The strategy was informed by an extensive public consultation involving artists, arts organisations, community groups, volunteers and members of the public.

Cathaoirleach of Galway County Council, Cllr Andrew Reddington (FG), said the plan recognised the central role the arts play in communities across the county. “Galway is a county with an extraordinary cultural identity, where creativity is woven into the fabric of our towns, villages, islands and Gaeltacht communities. This Arts Plan recognises the enormous contribution artists, volunteers, festivals and community groups make to county life and sets out a clear vision to support them over the next five years”.

He continued, “The arts bring people together, strengthen our communities and help define our sense of place. Through this plan, Galway County Council is committed to increasing opportunities for people of all ages and backgrounds to create, participate in and experience the arts in every part of County Galway.”

Chief Executive Liam Conneally said the strategy would help deliver stronger, more vibrant communities while supporting the county's wider economic and social development. “The Arts Plan provides a strong strategic framework that reflects the important role the arts play in building vibrant, resilient and inclusive communities. It aligns with the Council's wider ambitions for community development, wellbeing, placemaking and sustainable economic growth”.

“Successful delivery of this plan will depend on collaboration, and we look forward to continuing to work with artists, arts organisations, community groups, educational institutions and our many partners to ensure County Galway remains a place where creativity can flourish and where the benefits of the arts are accessible to everyone,” he stated.

Director of Services with responsibility for Cultural Services, Michael Owens, said the strategy would deliver long-term investment in artists, cultural infrastructure and local communities. “This plan has been shaped by extensive consultation with artists, arts organisations, community groups and the public. It responds directly to what we heard, with a strong focus on supporting artists, creating new arts spaces, broadening participation and making the arts more accessible across every part of the county.”

Arts Officer and Creative Ireland Coordinator Sharon O'Grady said the strategy builds on the achievements of the previous Arts Plan. “The previous Arts Plan delivered significant progress despite the challenges of the COVID-19pandemic. We strengthened supports for artists, invested in arts infrastructure, expanded festivals and community programmes, and developed strong partnerships across the county”.

“This new plan builds on that success and provides a clear roadmap for the next five years. It reflects what artists, communities and stakeholders told us during the consultation process and sets out ambitious but achievable actions to support creativity, strengthen cultural infrastructure and ensure more people can participate in and benefit from the arts,” she outlined.

Among the measures included in the strategy are increased funding for artists through grants and bursaries, additional residency opportunities, professional development programmes, greater support for artists working through Irish and investment in emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence. The plan also aims to address the shortage of arts infrastructure by developing new creative spaces, repurposing vacant buildings, strengthening festivals and performance venues, and delivering a flagship annual cultural event in different parts of the county. It also envisages Tuam becoming a long-term creative hub and the creation of a Cultural Arts Trail highlighting Galway's artistic and cultural heritage.

The Arts Plan is aligned with Galway County Council's Corporate Plan 2025-2029 and the Local Economic and Community Plan 2024-2030. Delivery will be monitored through annual implementation plans, with a mid-term review in 2028 and a full evaluation in 2030.
Further information is available at www.galway.ie.

arts.title: Scariff Harbour Festival goes down a storm yet again
arts.excerpt: LOCAL LANDMARKS, stories from behind shop counters in East Clare, the lure of the Irish language in East Belfast and stories from Palestine were among the highlights of yet another successful Scariff Harbour Festival.
arts.author: Páraic McMahon
arts.caption: Linda Ervine, MBE and Council of State Member with her husband Brian officially opening Scariff Harbour Festival 2026 at Scariff GAA Club on Friday evening. Photograph: Arthur Ellis.
body: LOCAL LANDMARKS, stories from behind shop counters in East Clare, the lure of the Irish language in East Belfast and stories from Palestine were among the highlights of yet another successful Scariff Harbour Festival.
Soft rain did not deter the sing along crowds swaying to the songs of popular balladeers ‘The Kilkennys’, so called after their home city, as they brought Scariff Harbour Festival 2026 to a close.

Earlier young hurlers from East Belfast in their yellow and black club jerseys tucked into generous portions of spaghetti bolognese in the GAA Hall, already hoping they can return to play in the Barry Nash Memorial hurling tournament with so many other clubs.

“This was heartening to hear,” said Mike Rodgers, Chair of Scariff Harbour Festival Committee “and an indication that the festival’s efforts to continue building genuine relationships with the north is making a difference,” he said. It was also confirmed by Kimberly Robertson, Chair of East Belfast GAA Club, who chaperoned the young hurlers during their visit to East Clare.

Bilingual speeches by on-stage guests gave due recognition to passionate advocate of the Irish language, and former Club President of East Belfast GAA, Linda Ervine MBE, when she opened this year’s Harbour Festival on Friday night. Cathaoirleach of Clare County Council, Cllr Joe Killeen (FF), Éanna Rowe of Waterways Ireland and Harry O’Meara, Festival Co-founder spoke of Linda Ervine’s unwavering commitment to promoting not only the Irish language but sporting culture in protestant east Belfast.

“I was introduced to the Irish language fifteen years ago,” she said. “I had never learned a language at school. In fact, I never really had any interest in learning another language. Then I got the opportunity to learn a cúpla focal and it changed my life. When I started learning Irish all those years ago, my husband Brian was the leader of the PUP, and there was quite a bit of media interest in the fact that his wife was learning Irish. The newspaper articles encouraged others from the local community to learn Irish too, so we set up our own classes and it just took off,” said the newly appointed Council of State Member.

In welcoming Linda and her husband Brian, local pharmacist Harry O’Meara acknowledged the festival’s strong connection with Northern Ireland and Linda’s on-going cultural work, born out of her initial and surprising attraction to the Irish language. “She founded Scoil na Seolta, the first integrated school in Northern Ireland to teach through the medium of Irish, and now manages the Turas Project, one of the largest providers of Irish language classes in Belfast,” he said. The event concluded with a moving rendition by Brian Ervine, former teacher, playwright and politician, of his own song Leaving Dal Riada

Tens of familiar faces from families of past Scariff shopkeepers could be spotted in an audience of over 150 people at an illustrated talk ‘Behind the Counter’ given by Dr. Jane Halloran-Ryan. In it, the Mary Immaculate College lecturer and professional genealogist traced the story of local shopkeepers and their significant role in the community to a highly engaged audience. “The study is definitely a work in progress,” she said.

The Camino of Hope walk snaked its pilgrim way in drizzly rain to the Mass Rock in Cappabane, led by the Bishop of Killaloe, Fintan Monahan and local Parish Priest, Fr. Pat Larkin, with ponder stops along the route. It concluded with the celebration of mass at the historic penal site to over 250 people before returning with the aid of their complimentary pilgrim sticks to the noise of the festival town.

Not the only nod to local history, brothers and local history aficionados Martin and Micheál Pearl led the increasingly popular 3km walk, highlighting the origins of Scariff and the landmark story points along the way.

Indoors a deeply moved audience became immersed in the personal journey to Palestine of local couple Bonnie Boyle and PJ McNamara through their film The Art of Resistance-The Art of Sumud. It was followed by a discussion, chaired by Jim Collins of Scariff Bay Community Radio, and included the profoundly touching contribution of Fatma Abuawwad, a Gazan woman and former school principal, who spent time with her family in Scariff after leaving Palestine to escape the ravages of war.

Don Stiffe and the Voices of Ireland got the festival off to a popular start with a concert in the Church of the Sacred Heart. The Family Fun Day in the GAA park thrilled the younger folk, while teenagers took to adrenalin fueled water-based activities and TV Chef, Shane Smith captivated an enthusiastic audience with his animated cookery demonstration.

The Festival Chair, Mike Rodgers acknowledged sponsors Waterways Ireland, EKO Integrated Services, Michael McNamara MEP (IND) and everyone who supported the festival and very specially the hardworking committee who deliver so successfully every year. “It could not happen without you all,” he said.
