arts.title: Ireland's leading aerial dance company to expand Parteen base & international reach
arts.excerpt: IRELAND’s leading aerial dance company, Fidget Feet, has unveiled a major growth strategy aimed at expanding its international presence while strengthening its creative base in Parteen.
arts.author: Páraic McMahon
body: IRELAND’s leading aerial dance company, Fidget Feet, has unveiled a major growth strategy aimed at expanding its international presence while strengthening its creative base in Parteen.

At the the 17th Irish Aerial Dance Festival in Letterkenny, Co Donegal which brings together aerial artists, performers and industry leaders from Ireland and overseas, the company launched its Fidget Feet Strategic Plan 2026-2029.

Plans to increase international touring, develop new creative partnerships and grow audiences at home and abroad as the organisation approaches its 30th anniversary in 2028 are set out in the three-year roadmap.

A key focus of the strategy will be establishing Limerick as Fidget Feet’s permanent creative hub, building on its base at the Irish Aerial Creation Centre at the former Burlington factory site in Parteen, near the University of Limerick.

Over the lifetime of the plan, the company said it aims to deliver more than 200 performances nationally and internationally, while expanding the Irish Aerial Dance Festival as a major showcase event for the artform. The company also intends to offer eight scholarships and an Emma Insley Commission worth €5,000 in 2029 to support emerging talent and new artistic work.

Founded in 1998 by Donegal native Chantal McCormick and her husband Jym Daly, Fidget Feet has become a leading force in aerial dance and contemporary circus, creating more than 38 productions and performing across Europe, North America, Australia, Africa and Asia.

Chairperson Gerard Dollard said the strategy marked a new chapter for the company. “Fidget Feet has spent almost three decades pushing artistic boundaries and creating opportunities for artists, audiences and communities across Ireland and internationally. This strategy provides a clear direction for the next stage of that journey, with strengthening our home in Limerick at the heart of our plans. We want to continue building a world-class creative base that supports artists, attracts international collaboration and showcases the very best of Irish aerial arts”.

Dollard who spent twenty years in a number of senior roles with Clare County Council including Deputy Chief Executive and Director of Service, said the timing of the launch during the Irish Aerial Dance Festival was significant. “The festival has become one of the most important gatherings for aerial arts in Europe and reflects the leadership role that Fidget Feet continues to play in developing the artform.”
Founder and Artistic Director Chantal McCormick said the company’s ambition from the beginning was to prove aerial performance could thrive in Ireland.

“When we started Fidget Feet, our ambition was to create extraordinary aerial performances that would inspire audiences while proving that this artform could flourish in Ireland. Almost three decades later, we’ve built something that reaches far beyond our own productions. We’ve helped create a thriving aerial arts community and supported artists who are now shaping the next generation of the sector. We want to create bold, world-class work that tours nationally and internationally, while continuing to mentor artists, foster collaboration and ensure Ireland is recognised as a global centre for aerial arts”.

Artistic work, people, roots and reach, and leadership and governance are the four key areas that the strategy focuses on. Fidget Feet said it will also prioritise audience development, inclusion, community engagement and financial sustainability as it prepares for its 30th anniversary celebrations in 2028 and the 20th anniversary of the Irish Aerial Dance Festival in 2029. The company is supported by the Arts Council, Limerick City and County Council, Donegal County Council, Clare County Council, Culture Ireland, the University of Limerick, the Irish Aerial Creation Centre, and the Irish Street Arts, Circus and Spectacle Network.

arts.title: 'Some musicians say their year wouldn't be the same if they didn't perform at the Feakle Festival'
arts.excerpt: FEAKLE is tuning up for the arrival of thousands of visitors across the next week.
arts.author: Páraic McMahon
arts.caption: Photograph: Ruthie Griffin.
body: FEAKLE is tuning up for the arrival of thousands of visitors across the next week.
Concerts, workshops, presentations and lively sessions galore await for the 39th Feakle Festival which kicks into gear on Wednesday (August 5th) and runs until Monday August 10th.

“There’s lots of things to expect from it whether you are a musician, dancer, a music lover or just coming to visit of Feakle in East Clare, there’s something for everyone,” explained Aoife Hayes who serves as secretary of the festival committee.

Tulla Céilí Band will hold eightieth anniversary celebrations at the community hall and will launch a CD. The festival itself begins by looking to the past and the future with a presentation by Tulla fiddler Sorcha Costelloe. The presentation titled, ‘Looking back while moving forward: The past, present and future of the East Clare Music Tradition’ takes place in the Community Hall at 19:30. “She will be doing a presentation on the night and has composed new music around the tradition, rhythm and style of East Clare music around the past”.

Workshops take place on Thursday, Friday and Saturday morning “with many fabulous tutors” including Martin Hayes, Jack Talty, Páraic Mac Donnchadha, Terence O'Reilly, Nuala Kennedy, Mary McNamara and Claire Keville.

Concerts “are nearly sold out and are at capacity,” Aoife outlined. Eva Carroll and Meabh Mulligan headline the Thursday night concert in Peppers, talented tutors will show how it's done with the Friday lunchtime concert while later that night Pepper's marquee will host Eleanor Shanley and Mike Hanrahan. Liam O’Connor and Cormac Begley are in St Mary's Church on Saturday night for a gala concert with the Community Hall serving as the setting for a céilí with The Star of Munster. The grand finale céilí celebrates eighty years of the Tulla Céilí Band on Sunday at the marquee in what promises to be “very special”.

Ninety years of the Tulla Pipe Band will also be marked. “They will march through the street during the festival, this was a thing of the past for committee to march behind him, there’s something special about that too for it to be happening and with their 90th anniversary,” Aoife maintained.

Having the festival in existence for thirty nine years is “incredible,” she told The Clare Echo. “There is something for everyone which is the beauty of it, if you stroll around the village if the weather permits you will find a beautiful atmosphere, it is something quite special to experience it. It amazes me to see people travelling from all over the world and how they can find the village of Feakle in East Clare by word of mouth, from people hearing positive things about it down through the years”.

Her uncle Martin, the gifted fiddler always draws a crowd with his appearances. The Hayes family have been associated with the festival for as long as Aoife can remember including the input of her father Pat on the committee. This is her fifth year on the committee but she has actively helped out behind the scenes long before then. “It is hard to pinpoint when my involvement with the festival started, growing up ten minutes down the road we were always there. My Dad was on the committee then and still is, it became a highlight for our year as children, it is a massive conversation at home, particularly for the last couple of months. As a teenager I got involved helping out in the office and that continued to where I am now with the committee as secretary. I’ve been more heavily involved in the last few years but I’ve always been helping out, I’m nearly thirty now but it has always been part of my life, it is hard to explain what the festival means to me, it is part of my identity and it becomes part of your life, I am immensely proud to have had the opportunity to be involved in it”.

Musicians travelled from as far away as Mozambique to attend the Feakle Festival last year. “We haven’t anything as far as Mozambique in the programme but I’m sure they will travel from near and far, it is incredible to see people come from near and far”.

Growth of the festival is visible each year, she said. “Each year it is exceeding our expectations and how it has developed with the programme expanding, it is nearly a week long festival and with the calibre of musicians that want to play in Feakle. We have high-end musicians known globally who are delighted and humbled to play at the Feakle Festival. Some musicians say their year wouldn’t be the same if they didn’t play in Feakle”.

Thousands of people are expected in East Clare for the festival. “It is hard to put an exact number on it but between 5,000 to 6,000 is the miniumum grasp of it. It is hard to pinpoint it, some have said 8,000 but it is tough to quantify because we have so many events. Tickets are selling incredibly well and we are anticipating a good crowd, hopefully the weather plays ball and people will come out to support the artists and East Clare businesses. It does have a knock-on effect to businesses and supports them whether it is a business owner with a restaurant, café and shop”.

She said there is a “huge” lift for the economy in Feakle and wider East Clare area thanks to the festival. “People are travelling, they need a bed rest and food so it boosts the local economy which is fantastic to see. We’re very fortunate to have four pubs running during the festival, a lot of businesses can make a lot of their income by having a festival running, it is important to thank them for allowing this to happen”.

arts.title: Scariff Bay & Raidió Corca Baiscinn strike gold at Craol awards
arts.excerpt: SCARIFF BAY Community Radio and Raidió Corca Baiscinn both struck gold at the Craol annual achievement awards. A total of five gold awards returned to Co Clare following the Craol Annual Achievement awards held at The Shamrock Hotel in Athlone last week with SBCR and RCB also winning standout submission awards. The awards celebrate the work of all community radio stations in Ireland highlighting the roles that community radio plays in promoting local voices and inclusion all over the country.
arts.author: Páraic McMahon
body: SCARIFF BAY Community Radio and Raidió Corca Baiscinn both struck gold at the Craol annual achievement awards. A total of five gold awards returned to Co Clare following the Craol Annual Achievement awards held at The Shamrock Hotel in Athlone last week with SBCR and RCB also winning standout submission awards. The awards celebrate the work of all community radio stations in Ireland highlighting the roles that community radio plays in promoting local voices and inclusion all over the country.
This year having recently been given a full ten year broadcasting license by Coimisiún na Meán, Scariff Bay Community Radio (SBCR) were eligible to enter three categories.

Under Social Benefit – Music Category the SBCR entry was a two hour live broadcast presented by Tulla’s Daragh Leamy from Scoil Samhraidh Willie Clancy. “I’m delighted to get recognition for talking trad, programme which is well liked by our listeners. Presenting live from the Willie Clancy Festival was a particular thrill and we had a wide range range of guests and musicians both young and old”.

Monthly Irish programme Gaeilge agus Fáilte presented by Bernadette Watson was nominated under the Irish Language Category and was the winner of a gold award. “Ni Heart go cure le cheile- Ta ríméad orm an gradam seo a bhuacaint. This programme was a very special edition as I was interviewing three women new to the country who were enthusiastically learning the language, all of whom have come to live in Clare from different corners of the world,” she stated.

An in-depth programme titled ‘Domestic Abuse – The Hidden Plague in our Society’ received gold in the Social Benefit: Talk category. It had a wide range of contributors of Social Workers and members of An Garda Siochana outlining the services available to victims and how to recognise the signs of Domestic Abuse. “It was amazing to win a gold award but to win a standout achievement award on top of that is the icing on the cake. Geraldine and myself both went way out of our comfort zone to research and make this programme. We wanted to have the right people to give the right information in a sensitive and accessible manner. Particular thanks to our guests on the programme and a big thank you to our station manager for allowing us to us to make this programme,” Feakle woman Marianne said.

Geraldine added, “This programme was a long time in the making. Our guests were specialists in their chosen fields and really the programme was steered by their input. To win an outstanding achievement award is a great recognition for the radio and the quality of programming that our volunteers produce on a weekly basis”. RCB's total tally of Craol awards has now jumped to thirty following their latest success. The two-part documentary, ‘In My Father’s House’ won gold in the Irish Culture Showcase category. Three generations of the Killeen family from Cree featured in the documentary. It examined the family history through song, poetry, dance and music over the past eighty years in West Clare through the voice of Francis Killeen who has lived in this area since he was born and has reared his family.

In the Social Benefit: Music category, RCB took the top prize for Viktotiia’s weekly playlist. This unique show is aimed at fostering community ties as well as celebrating diversity through music. It is Viktoriia’s way of connecting people through music and stories and turn an ordinary afternoon into a musical journey.

Station manager with RCB, Máiréad O’Higgins Finnegan said, “I am delighted that we have received two more gold awards, and it is a testament to the hard work of the wonderful and talented staff and volunteers here at Raidió Corca Baiscinn”. She added, “These awards recognise the valuable contribution everyone at the Station has made to our varied and wide programme of entertaining broadcasts over the last twenty six years”.

Jim Collins, co-founder and station manager of Scariff Bay Radio commented, “We are thrilled to win three golds and a standout submission award in our first full year as a fully licensed community radio station. These wins are a tribute to the 95 volunteers who contribute on a weekly basic and make Scariff Bay Community radio the success that it has become. We want to bring the best range of quality programming to our listeners and this year’s success is a sign that we are going in the right direction”.

arts.title: Scariff couple share experiences from Palestine in new film
arts.excerpt: EXPERIENCES from Palestine by a Scariff couple will be shared in a short film.
arts.author: Páraic McMahon
body: EXPERIENCES from Palestine by a Scariff couple will be shared in a short film.
Bonnie Boyle and PJ McNamara had for years been talking about ways to try directly support the people of Palestine while also showing their quiet solidarity.

In 2022, Bonnie and PJ made the trip to Palestine where they put together a short film ‘The Art of Resistance: The Art of Sumud’ which will be screened at the Scariff Harbour Festival at 5pm on Saturday August 1st.
Following the screening, there will be a discussion at the GAA half with PJ, Bonnie and Fatma Abuawwad, a woman from Gaza, who lived in Scariff for a time before moving with her family to Dublin.

Sumud is a core cultural value and ideology representing everyday resistance, rootedness and determination by Palestinians to remain on their land and maintain dignity despite ongoing oppression and hardship. The film was recently screened at the Belltable in Limerick and at venues in Cork, Dublin, Athlone and as far away as Chicago.

Speaking ahead of the screening in Scariff, Bonnie stated, “PJ and I had thought many times about volunteering in Palestine in the hope that we could get a better understanding of life for Palestinians and contribute in some small way to the people we met. “I had found an artisan craft worker who had put us in touch with Palestinian women who made traditional crafts and PJ had connected with an olive oil trader, but the accidental film ultimately became more about our journey to places like Bethlehem, Dheisheh, Jerusalem, Ramallah and Hebron, names all too familiar to us now”.

Neither Bonnie nor PJ were professional filmmakers. Something struck them immediately about the people they met that felt compelling. It was only when they came across the term Sumud they began to understand that resilience was at the heart of everything the Palestinians said and did and was strikingly evident in their day-to-day life. It became the spark that ignited the film, but neither was, at that time, aware how the landscape in Palestine would change or how the weight of editing their simple film would become increasingly heavy.

Before the war in Gaza, Fatma dedicated her career to educating and helping young people build their futures. Having been displaced by the war, she and her family came to Ireland in January 2024. Like many forced to leave their homes, she had to adapt to a different culture, language and way of life. “Rebuilding a life after war is not only about finding safety- it is also about re discovering purpose and hope,” said the former Gazan school principal.

Living with the emotional impact of war and the uncertainty of the future are still significant challenges for the Abuawwad family to overcome. Starting a completely new life in a country with different systems and ways of doing things requires constant adjustment. Despite having extensive leadership experience in education, Fatma still strives to rebuild a professional identity.

She turned down an offer of a full-time job with Amazon to take care of her family, but she has now started a small handmade soap business from scratch, introducing a traditional Palestinian product to a new market. “Although still coping with the loss of familiarity and trying to create a sense of belonging in Ireland, preserving my Palestinian identity and cultural heritage is still hard but I continue to believe and hope in the opportunities to come,” Fatma said

arts.title: Summer Fest to see Ruan roar to life
arts.excerpt: RUAN is set to roar to life with the inaugural Summer Fest taking over the village for the August Bank Holiday weekend.
arts.author: Páraic McMahon
arts.caption: The five-person committee behind the Ruan Summer Fest.
body: RUAN is set to roar to life with the inaugural Summer Fest taking over the village for the August Bank Holiday weekend.
Across Saturday (August 1st) and Sunday (August 2nd), Ruan will play host to music concerts and family fun with a festival for the whole community.

With the Custys and Shannons, Ruan, Dysart and Toonagh can lay claim to having some fine musical pedigree down through the generations. Harping into that tradition, Electrad lead the Saturday evening concert with Ennis’ Dave Hanrahan formerly of The Riordan and The Swoonies also taking to the stage. Hermitage Green are the headline act for the Sunday show, the concert will be opened up by Shannon’s Adam Moloney with Ennis alternative female band Social Dilemma also entertaining crowds.

There will be a family fun day from 12pm to 5pm on Sunday with face painting, a petting zoo, reptile show, tug of war, long puc, children’s disco, stalls from local traders and a novel golf ball release race.

A five-person committee has been in place since last October to make Ruan Summer Fest a reality. The committee consists of Gavin McGibney (Chairperson), Sheena Rice, Josephine Taaffe, Conor Reeves and John Punch.

Speaking to The Clare Echo, John said a conversation last autumn led to the group coming together. “A lot of other parishes are doing something similar and are having events for parish so we said it would be nice to have an event for Ruan and it grew legs from there”.

He continued, “We have set it up as a community event ran by the community but we’re open to everybody and anybody to come along. Hopefully we will get the weather and that the event goes well, it might be something we could do as an annual event depending on whether it is a success or not”. Punch added, “We’ve capacity of 1000 per night, we’d be hoping to sell it out as best we can. It would be great, we’ve a fantastic line-up and some local artists with headline bands, it would be nice to fill it out”.

Páirc na Gael, the home of Ruan GAA will be the setting for the marquee for both concerts. “The local GAA club have been very good to us, it is not a club ran event so we had to go to them and see if they could facilitate us. They were very good and forthcoming, they are giving us the training field and we’ll have the marquee set up there,” John outlined.

Tickets can be purchased online at ruansummerfest.ie, they will also be on sale outside XL Ruan this Sunday from 11am to 1pm. A weekend pass costs €60, tickets for the Hermitage Green concert are €40 and the Electrad gig is €30.

Funds raised will be given back to the community, Punch stated. “You have the clubs based within community, the GAA club for giving us grounds will get something, Ruan camogie club, the old folks group who have their Christmas get-together, the Tidy Towns who are doing fantastic work and our local scouts who are working just outside the village in the scout camp”.

Feakle native John who won a Clare IHC with Ruan in 2012 is hopeful the festival will make more people aware of the village and what it has to offer. “The plan is for the whole community to benefit, it is a community event ran by the community. We’ve a lot of good volunteers putting their names forward. Ruan is a close-knit community and there are a lot of good things about it, the shop has reopened and it has brought vibrancy to the village, the hurling club is the focal point but we have other activities and we want to get the word out that Ruan is a good place”.

He added, “there’s a great history of music in the parish”. He said, “The reopening of the shop has brought a vibrant feel to the centre of the village, if it is a success it will promote Ruan as a nice spot. We’ve one of the nicest forest walks in Dromore beside us, it will be nice to sit outside in this weather and take in what the village has to offer”.

Part of the fun will be a novel golf ball release race. “It is something different, we’re asking people to come along and buy a golf ball, the first golf ball to cross the hill will win a prize. It will start from the top of the hill coming into the village from the Ennis side, we’re not sure exactly where the finish line will be. The roads into the village will be closed off coming into it, we’ll have car parks and detours, it will be nice and safe for children to run around the village”.

Closing off the roads was one of the first targets of the committee, John recalled. “It was the first thing we decided to do was to try get the road closure to make it as safe as possible and get as many families in. We’re running from two different locations, it is a short walk to the shop from where some other activities going on, it was safer to close it off and we’ve thankfully managed to do that”.
